No Result View All Result Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us Hausa Edition Home News Politics Business Sport Football Health Entertainment Education Opinion Editorial Columns Others LeVogue Magazine Conferences National Economy Contact Us No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Nigeria’s Care Economy To Generate 17m Jobs, $9.3bn GDP – FG by Olushola Bello 11 minutes ago in Business Share on WhatsApp Share on Facebook Share on X Telegram The federal government has said Nigeria’s care economy could generate between 9.4 million and 17 million jobs and contribute at least $9.3 billion to the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP), as it moves to address gaps in childcare and other care services.
The government said expanding access to universal childcare and closing the country’s care gaps would unlock significant economic opportunities, particularly for women, who account for between 57 and 67 per cent of the projected jobs.
Speaking at the National Care Forum, themed, ‘Advancing Nigeria’s Care Economy: Jobs, Growth & Productivity’, held on Tuesday in Lagos, the Director of Child Development, Federal Ministry of Women Affairs, Mr. Ali Madugu, who represented the Minister, Hajia Iman Sulaiman-Ibrahim, disclosed that the Federal Executive Council (FEC) approved the National Care Policy and Implementation Plan 2026-2030 on October 28. He said the policy was designed to address the country’s care deficit, create employment opportunities and improve women’s participation in the economy.
Madugu added that every $1 invested in childcare could generate $3 in economic returns.
Earlier, the Head of Office, Nigeria, International Finance Corporation (IFC), Mr. Christian Mulamula, said Nigeria could unlock up to $22.9 billion in annual GDP by closing its gender gap in care.
Describing care as economic infrastructure rather than merely a family responsibility, Mulamula said Nigerian women spend approximately three times as much time on unpaid care work as men, a situation that pushes many out of the workforce.
He said about 67 per cent of working parents believed they would be more productive if they had better access to quality childcare. “How do we build a care economy that works for our children, for our families, for our businesses, and for Nigeria’s growth?” he asked.
He said investment in quality early childhood programmes could yield returns of up to 13 per cent annually and raise Nigeria’s total factor productivity by as much as two per cent.
According to him, 92 per cent of childcare facilities in Nigeria are small and independently owned, while 76 per cent of childcare entrepreneurs lack access to formal financing.
Representing the Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, the Commissioner for Finance, Mr. Abayomi Oluyomi, said the state had identified care as a priority under its Women Economic Empowerment Policy Roadmap and was developing an investment-oriented care policy framework.
He said the state government was working towards building a care economy where families could access reliable and affordable services, care providers could operate viable businesses, and workers in the sector could earn decent livelihoods.
Oluyomi, however, warned that government funding alone would not be sufficient to meet the growing demand for care services.
Citing Lagos State’s infrastructure financing gap of over N10 trillion against a budget of N4.4 trillion, he said the government needed to establish appropriate regulations, standards and an enabling business environment to attract private investors while ensuring affordability.
Also speaking, the Director, Special Duties, Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, Dr. Gloria Ahmed, said care must be integrated into national and state development plans and budgets.
She stressed the need for clear responsibilities, effective coordination and accountability to ensure that the National Care Policy did not become another well-articulated policy without adequate funding.
On workforce development and professional standards, the Director, National Board for Technical Education (NBTE), Engineer Sulaiman Yusuf, said the care sector must move beyond its largely informal structure.
He disclosed that Nigeria had developed National Occupational Standards for childcare workers, adding that more than 4,500 caregivers, 90 per cent of them women, were already undergoing training.
Yusuf called for the establishment of a strong sectoral body to professionalise the workforce without excluding existing informal care workers.
Similarly, the UN Women Representative, Ms. Beatrice Eyong, said while unpaid care work was largely undertaken by women, the paid care economy remained dominated by men, with women-led care businesses facing informality and limited access to finance.
She called for the provision of labour-saving devices for rural women, improved financial inclusion for women entrepreneurs and greater involvement of men in sharing household care responsibilities.
